title: Julius Caesar (Acts I and II)
author: William Shakespeare
tagline: Play · Shakespearean tragedy · ambition, honour and the making of a conspiracy

overview.intro: Rome is celebrating. Julius Caesar has returned in triumph after defeating the sons of his old rival Pompey, and many citizens want to see him crowned. Others fear that the Republic, in which power was shared, is about to be replaced by the rule of one man. In Acts I and II, the envious and clever Cassius draws the respected Brutus into a plot against Caesar; omens fill the sky, warnings are ignored, and by the end of Act II the conspirators are ready and Caesar has been persuaded to walk into the Senate. These two acts are about how a plot is born: through persuasion, doubt, flattery and the fear of tyranny.

blocks.text: William Shakespeare wrote Julius Caesar around 1599, at the height of his career, and it was staged in the open-air Globe theatre in London. The story is based on real events. Shakespeare took most of his material from Plutarch, a Greek writer who wrote short biographies of famous Greeks and Romans, in the English translation by Sir Thomas North. Shakespeare shapes this material for the stage: he compresses time, invents conversations and sharpens the characters, so the play is drama built on history, not a history lesson.

Historical context. Rome had long been a republic, ruled by elected officials and the Senate, and Romans were proud that they had once driven out their kings. Julius Caesar was a brilliant general who rose above all rivals. After a civil war he defeated Pompey, once his ally and then his enemy, and later defeated Pompey's sons. The play opens as Caesar comes back to Rome after this last victory. To his admirers he is the saviour of Rome. To his critics he has grown too powerful, and they suspect that he wants the title of king, which would end the Republic.

The Elizabethan audience. Shakespeare's first audiences were English people who lived under a queen with no children. They were anxious about who would rule after her, and about civil war. Many believed strongly in order in the state and in nature, in omens and in the influence of fate. A play in which a ruler is challenged, the heavens seem to protest and the state is thrown into danger spoke directly to those fears. Shakespeare also leaves the audience free to judge: he gives Caesar real faults and the conspirators real reasons, so neither side is simply good or simply evil.
The central question of Acts I and II is whether it can ever be right to kill a ruler for the sake of liberty, and what happens to a good man when he lets others persuade him to do so.

items.term: Scene i: a street in Rome
items.meaning: Two tribunes, Flavius and Marullus, find crowds of commoners in holiday clothes, ready to cheer Caesar's triumph. A cobbler and a carpenter answer the tribunes with jokes and word-play, which is one reason these speeches are in prose. Marullus scolds the crowd angrily: they cheered Pompey in the same way, and now they celebrate the man who has defeated Pompey's sons. Ashamed, the commoners slip away. Flavius sends Marullus to strip the decorations from Caesar's statues, and says that if Caesar's rise is checked, he will stay an ordinary man instead of soaring out of sight. The scene tells us at once that Rome is divided over Caesar, and that the crowd is easily swayed. It is also the day of the feast of Lupercal, a festival in Rome.

items.term: Scene ii, part 1: the procession and the warning
items.meaning: Caesar enters with his wife Calpurnia, Antony, Brutus, Cassius, Casca and others, for the festival races. He asks Antony to touch Calpurnia as he runs, because the old belief is that this will cure childlessness, and Antony promises to do as Caesar says. A soothsayer calls out from the crowd, warning Caesar to beware the Ides of March (the fifteenth of March). Caesar looks at him, calls him a dreamer, and moves on. The warning is ignored, which is exactly what the audience will remember later.

items.term: Scene ii, part 2: Cassius works on Brutus
items.meaning: Brutus stays behind with Cassius, saying he does not care for the games. Cassius says Brutus has become distant and unfriendly. Brutus replies that he is troubled by conflicting thoughts of his own, not by any coldness towards his friend. Cassius uses this moment. He tells Brutus that the Romans respect him, that Caesar is a man like any other, and he offers two stories of Caesar's weakness: once, when they swam in the river Tiber, Caesar nearly drowned and called to Cassius for help, and once, when he had a fever in Spain, he shook and cried out like a sick girl. Cassius then says that Caesar now strides over the world like a huge statue while others creep beneath him, and that it is not fate but their own weakness that allows this. Loud shouts are heard from offstage, and Brutus fears that the people are choosing Caesar as their king. He admits that he loves Caesar, but adds that he loves honour more, and that he does not want a king in Rome. Cassius has found what he needs.

items.term: Scene ii, part 3: Caesar on Cassius, and Casca's report
items.meaning: Caesar returns, looking disturbed. He notices Cassius and tells Antony that he does not trust him: Cassius looks thin and hungry, thinks too much, watches everyone closely and does not enjoy plays or music, and men like this are dangerous. Caesar adds that he is not afraid, since he is Caesar, and asks Antony to walk on his right side because he is deaf in that ear. The others hold Casca back to hear what happened. In a bluntly mocking prose speech, Casca tells them that Antony three times offered Caesar a crown; each time Caesar pushed it away, though each refusal seemed to Casca half-hearted, and each time the crowd roared. Then Caesar fell down in the marketplace, foaming at the mouth and unable to speak; he suffers from the falling sickness, that is, epilepsy. When he recovered he apologised to the crowd. Casca also says that Flavius and Marullus were silenced for pulling decorations off the statues. Brutus goes home, promising to talk to Cassius again soon. Left alone, Cassius says aloud that Brutus is noble but can be turned from his nature, and that he will throw forged letters, written in different hands as if by many citizens, into Brutus's window that night.

items.term: Scene iii: a street, night, thunder and lightning
items.meaning: A wild storm is raging. Cicero and Casca meet. Casca is frightened by what he has seen: a fire in the sky, a slave whose hand burned without harm, a lion wandering the streets and an owl hooting at noon. Cicero says that people read omens their own way and leaves. Cassius, who walks through the storm with his chest bared, reads the omens as warnings from the gods about the danger Caesar poses, not as terror. He and Casca speak openly, and Casca says that the Senate means to make Caesar king the next day. Casca joins the plot. Cinna, another conspirator, arrives, and Cassius gives him letters to place where Brutus will find them. Cassius says that with Brutus on their side the plot will look honourable. The act ends with the plotters hoping to win Brutus to their side before the night is over.

Brutus cannot sleep. In a soliloquy he argues himself into the plot. He has no personal grievance against Caesar, he says, but the general good demands that Caesar be stopped, and it must be by his death. He fears that power will change Caesar, as a snake is harmless until warmed by the sun, and that it is safest to deal with the danger before it hatches. His servant Lucius brings him a letter found in the window, and Brutus reads it as a call from Rome to act. Lucius also tells him that the next day is the fifteenth of March. The conspirators arrive, their faces hidden in their cloaks: Cassius, Casca, Decius, Cinna, Metellus Cimber and Trebonius. They plan to strike the next day at the Senate. Cassius proposes an oath; Brutus refuses, saying that a good cause needs no oath and that Romans who are honourable keep their word without one. Metellus suggests inviting the elderly Cicero, but Brutus says Cicero will never follow anything begun by others, so he is left out. Cassius wants to kill Antony too, but Brutus refuses: they must be sacrificers, not butchers, and Antony alone, he says, cannot do much harm. Cassius worries that Caesar may not go to the Senate because of his growing belief in omens; Decius says he will manage this by flattery. The plotters leave at dawn.

Brutus's wife Portia comes to him, worried that he has been restless, silent and distant for days. She kneels and begs him to trust her. She proves that she can keep a secret by pointing to a wound she gave herself in the thigh. Brutus is moved and promises to tell her everything later. Caius Ligarius, a sick Roman with a grudge against Caesar, arrives at the door. He says he will follow Brutus to any deed, and they go out together.

It is the night of the storm and Caesar cannot sleep. His wife Calpurnia has cried out three times in her sleep that Caesar is being murdered. She begs him not to leave the house that day, and points to the terrible omens in the streets. Caesar first refuses: he says cowards die many times before they die, while a brave man dies only once, and that death will come when it will come. A servant returns from the priests, who report that the animal they sacrificed had no heart, a terrible sign. Caesar brushes this aside too, but Calpurnia begs on her knees and he agrees to stay at home, sending Antony to tell the Senate that he is ill. Decius Brutus arrives to escort him to the Senate. Caesar tells him he will not come and offers no reason but his will; then, softening, he tells him Calpurnia's dream of a statue of Caesar with a hundred spouts running with blood, and Romans smiling as they bathed their hands in it. Decius cleverly explains the dream in Caesar's favour: Rome, he says, will draw new life from Caesar. He adds that the Senate plans to offer Caesar a crown that day and might change its mind if he stays away, and that people would laugh at him for listening to a woman's fears. Caesar gives in, tells Calpurnia that her fears now seem foolish, and goes out with the conspirators who have come to greet him. Brutus, one of them, says quietly to himself that it pains him to think how they are friends only in appearance.

items.term: Scene iii: a street near the Capitol
items.meaning: Artemidorus, a teacher, reads aloud the letter he has written to Caesar. It names the conspirators one by one and warns Caesar to beware of them, for they are of one mind against him. He will hand it to Caesar as he passes and hopes that Caesar will read it. The scene is very short, but it is a moment of tension: the audience sees that the danger has been named.

Portia is close to breaking down. She sends Lucius to the Senate, then can barely say why, and cries out that it is hard for women to keep a secret. The soothsayer appears and says he means to stand where Caesar will pass and try to speak to him; he fears that some harm may come to Caesar. Portia is left frightened and helpless, praying that her husband's plan will succeed.

blocks.text: Where Act II leaves us: Brutus has committed himself, the plot is organised, and Caesar has ignored the warnings of his wife, the priests, the soothsayer and Artemidorus. What follows in the later acts is the result of these choices.

items.meaning: The most powerful man in Rome, a great general newly returned in triumph. He is confident, proud and sometimes vain: he often speaks of himself as 'Caesar' in the third person, as if he were a monument. He has bodily weaknesses (deafness in one ear and epilepsy) that Cassius mocks. He refuses the crown in public, yet he ignores the soothsayer and later gives way to flattery. He is a mixture of real strength and dangerous overconfidence, and he shows the very qualities the conspirators fear.

A respected Roman noble, known for his honour and for his family's history of resisting kings. He is thoughtful, idealistic and a lover of philosophy. He loves Caesar as a friend but loves Rome more, and in his orchard soliloquy he persuades himself to act on what might happen instead of what has happened. He is trusting: he refuses an oath, rejects Cicero and spares Antony. His goodness is what makes the conspiracy look respectable, and also what makes his judgement unreliable.

The moving spirit behind the plot. He is lean, intense, clever and envious, and Caesar rightly calls him dangerous. He reads people well and knows how to flatter Brutus, tempt Casca and use the storm as a sign. He is practical where Brutus is idealistic: he wants an oath, he wants Antony dead, and he is willing to use forged letters. He resents having to bow to a man he thinks is no better than himself.

Caesar's close friend and loyal follower, a sportsman who enjoys plays, music and company. In these acts he runs in the festival race and offers Caesar the crown at the Lupercal. He is not yet a major speaker, but Cassius considers him dangerous and wants him killed, while Brutus thinks he is a mere limb of Caesar and spares him.

A blunt-speaking Roman who pretends to be rougher and less intelligent than he is. His prose account of the crown being offered is full of contempt for the crowd and for Caesar. In the storm scene he is shaken and afraid, and Cassius easily draws him into the plot.

Caesar's wife. She is frightened by her dream and the omens, and she pleads with him not to leave home. She loves her husband and cares for his safety, and she is the first person to persuade him. Her warning is turned against her by Decius.

Brutus's wife, the daughter of a famous Roman, Cato. She is brave and loving, insists on being trusted and proves her strength by wounding herself. In Act II, scene iv, she is nearly overcome by fear that she will give away her husband's secret.

A member of the conspiracy who is chosen to bring Caesar to the Senate. He is a skilful flatterer. He knows Caesar's weak points, his pride and his fear of being thought afraid, and uses them to overturn Calpurnia's dream.

A fortune-teller who warns Caesar to beware the Ides of March. He is ignored by Caesar, but returns in Act II, scene iv, and tells Portia that he will try to speak to Caesar again. He represents fate's warning.

Officials who protect the rights of the common people. They rebuke the crowd for cheering Caesar and pull decorations off his statues. They show that not everyone in Rome accepts Caesar's growing power, and they are silenced for it, which shows that Caesar's power is real.

The conspirators fear Caesar's ambition and Cassius's own envy is at work as well. Brutus argues that power changes people. But the play also asks who is really ambitious: Caesar, who may want a crown, or Cassius, who resents another man's greatness?

Brutus is torn between his affection for Caesar and his sense of duty to Rome. He chooses public honour over private friendship. The struggle is at the heart of his soliloquy. It also shows how the word 'honour' can be used to justify wrong acts.

Cassius argues that people are responsible for their own fortunes, not the stars. Caesar says that death will come when it will come. The play asks whether events are fixed by fate or shaped by human choices, and both the plotters and Caesar make choices that push events forward.

The storm, the lion, the burning hand, Calpurnia's dream and the sacrifice without a heart are all read differently by different people. Casca is terrified, Cicero doubtful, Cassius uses them for his purposes, and Caesar hesitates and then dismisses them. Belief and doubt are both shown to be dangerous.

Acts I and II are full of people persuading each other: Cassius wins Brutus with flattery and forged letters, Brutus persuades himself with a clever argument, Calpurnia persuades Caesar to stay, and Decius persuades him to go. The play shows how easily a good argument can hide a bad cause.

The tribunes, Cassius and Brutus fear that Caesar will make himself king. The play never settles whether he really wanted a crown. It shows the fear of tyranny, the value of shared government and the dangers of acting violently in its defence.

A speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud, alone on stage. Brutus's soliloquy in the orchard (II.i) shows him reasoning towards the decision to act. Cassius also speaks alone at the end of I.ii to reveal his plan to forge letters. Soliloquies give the audience information the other characters do not have.

The audience knows more than a character. We know the fate that the soothsayer hints at, and we watch Caesar dismiss the warning. Caesar's speech about not fearing death is more powerful because we know how close the danger is. He also greets his enemies as friends and invites them to drink with him.

Events hint at what is coming: the soothsayer's warning, Calpurnia's dream of blood, the storm, the lifeless sacrificial animal, Artemidorus's letter and Portia's fear all prepare the audience for a disaster.

Thunder, lightning and strange sights in I.iii, and the restless night of II.i and II.ii, show that the natural world is disturbed just as Rome is. Shakespeare's audience believed that events in nature reflected events in the state. The storm also mirrors the storm inside Brutus.

Brutus is idealistic, principled and reluctant; Cassius is practical, envious and eager. Brutus refuses an oath and wants to spare Antony; Cassius wants both. The contrast shows two kinds of conspirator and why their union is uneasy.

Nobles usually speak blank verse, which gives their speeches dignity. The commoners in I.i speak prose, full of jokes. Casca's account of the crown in I.ii is also in prose, which fits his blunt, mocking tone and lowers the tone of the events he describes.

Cassius pictures Caesar as a giant statue standing over the world while others walk beneath him, an image of unnatural greatness. Brutus compares Caesar to a serpent's egg that should be crushed before it hatches. Such images shape how the audience sees Caesar.

learn.title: Tips for answering questions on the play

items: For an extract question, say who is speaking, to whom, where in the play (act and scene), and what has just happened before you explain the lines.
Explain meaning first, in your own words, then comment on the significance: what does the passage tell us about the character, the theme or what will happen next?
Back every claim about a character with an action or speech from Acts I and II, not from later in the play. If a question stays within these acts, do not bring in the assassination or its aftermath.
Do not paint Brutus as a villain or Caesar as a saint. The best answers show that both are mixtures of good and bad qualities.
For character comparisons, use a clear structure: two or three points of contrast, each supported by a specific moment (for example, the oath, Antony, Cicero).
For theme questions, name the theme, give two or three scenes as evidence, and finish with your own judgement.
Use short quotations sparingly and accurately. It is better to paraphrase than to quote wrongly.
Use the present tense when you describe what happens in the play.

keyPoints: Caesar returns in triumph after defeating Pompey's sons; Rome is divided between those who admire him and those who fear he will become king.
The tribunes Flavius and Marullus rebuke the commoners for cheering Caesar so soon after cheering Pompey.
A soothsayer warns Caesar to beware the Ides of March; Caesar dismisses him as a dreamer.
Cassius works on Brutus with flattery and stories of Caesar's weakness, and Brutus admits he loves honour more than his friend.
Casca reports that Antony offered Caesar the crown three times and that Caesar refused it each time, then fell down in a fit.
Caesar distrusts Cassius because he 'thinks too much'; Cassius plans forged letters to win Brutus.
The storm and omens of I.iii are read as warnings by some and used as tools by Cassius.
In his orchard soliloquy Brutus decides that Caesar must die for the general good, not for any personal grievance.
Brutus refuses an oath, rejects Cicero and spares Antony, decisions that show his idealism.
Calpurnia's dream and the omens nearly keep Caesar at home, but Decius's flattery persuades him to go to the Senate.
Artemidorus's warning letter and Portia's anxiety keep the sense of danger high at the end of Act II.
examFocus: Character sketches of Caesar, Brutus and Cassius, with evidence from Acts I and II.
The contrast between Brutus and Cassius, and why Cassius needs Brutus in the plot.
Brutus's orchard soliloquy: his reasoning and its weakness.
The soothsayer's warning and the use of omens, dreams and the storm.
Caesar's refusal of the crown and Casca's account of it.
Why Caesar decides to go to the Senate: Calpurnia's dream, Decius's arguments and Caesar's pride.
The role of Portia and Calpurnia.
Extract questions from the scenes with the soothsayer, Cassius and Brutus, and Caesar's speech on death.
Themes of honour, ambition, fate and republic versus tyranny, with references to specific scenes.

vocabulary.meaning: a person who claims to foretell the future
vocabulary.context: The soothsayer shouts a warning at Caesar in the crowd, but Caesar treats it as the babbling of a dreamer.

vocabulary.meaning: in the Roman calendar, the middle day of the month; in March, the fifteenth
vocabulary.context: The Ides of March is the date the soothsayer warns of, and the day on which the Senate is to meet.

vocabulary.meaning: a Roman official chosen to protect the interests of the common people
vocabulary.context: The tribunes Flavius and Marullus are angry that the crowd is so quick to honour Caesar.

vocabulary.meaning: a priest who studies signs such as the insides of sacrificed animals to foretell what will happen
vocabulary.context: The augurers report that the animal they sacrificed had no heart, and Calpurnia takes this as a sign of danger.

vocabulary.meaning: a sign that something important, usually bad, is going to happen
vocabulary.context: Casca sees the strange sights of the stormy night as portents of disaster for Rome.
Caesar points out Cassius across the crowd with the word yond, marking him out as a man to watch.
Cassius says Caesar doth stand over the world like a giant, using an old form of the verb 'does'.

vocabulary.meaning: old words for 'you' when speaking to one person, used among friends, family or inferiors
vocabulary.context: Portia uses thou and thee when she pleads with her husband, showing how close they are.

vocabulary.meaning: fond of games and sports; playful
vocabulary.context: Brutus tells Cassius that he is not gamesome, and so he stays away from the races.

vocabulary.meaning: slavery; the state of being under another's control
vocabulary.context: Cassius feels that living under Caesar's greatness is a kind of bondage, and this feeling drives him.

vocabulary.meaning: a person of lower rank who must obey others
vocabulary.context: Cassius tells Brutus that men are underlings by their own weakness, not because the stars have made them so.

vocabulary.meaning: to tolerate or put up with
vocabulary.context: Brutus says that an ancestor of his would not have tolerated a king in Rome, and he cannot brook it either.

vocabulary.meaning: to reject with scorn; to kick against
vocabulary.context: Brutus says he has no personal reason to spurn Caesar, meaning he holds no private grudge against him.

vocabulary.meaning: firmness and steadiness of mind; the ability to endure and keep faith
vocabulary.context: Portia wounds herself to prove her constancy, so that Brutus will trust her with his secret.

vocabulary.meaning: something breathed or given off; here, a meteor or shooting star
vocabulary.context: In the dark orchard, Brutus reads his letter by the light of the exhalations flashing across the night sky.

questions.prompt: Why do the tribunes Flavius and Marullus scold the commoners at the start of the play?
options: The commoners are breaking the law by holding a festival
The commoners are refusing to work for Caesar
The commoners are celebrating Caesar's triumph over Pompey's sons after once cheering Pompey
The commoners are plotting to make Antony king
questions.answer: The commoners are celebrating Caesar's triumph over Pompey's sons after once cheering Pompey.
questions.explanation: Marullus is angry at the crowd's disloyalty and how quickly its affections change. The scene shows Caesar's popularity and the tribunes' unease.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking the tribunes are Caesar's supporters. They oppose the show of honour to him.

questions.prompt: Who describes to Brutus and Cassius how Antony offered the crown to Caesar three times?
options: Cinna
Trebonius
Decius
Casca
questions.answer: Casca.
questions.explanation: Casca tells the story in a mocking prose speech in I.ii after Caesar leaves the stage.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the account to Cassius, who is standing beside Brutus.

questions.prompt: How does Cassius plan to win Brutus to the conspiracy?
options: By paying him a large sum of money
By throwing forged letters, written in different hands as if from citizens, into his window
By threatening to reveal a secret about his family
By asking Caesar to insult him in public
questions.answer: By throwing forged letters, written in different hands as if from citizens, into his window.
questions.explanation: At the end of I.ii Cassius tells the audience that he will make Brutus believe that Rome is calling on him to act. In I.iii he gives Cinna such letters to place.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking Brutus is persuaded only by Cassius's speeches; the letters are equally important.

questions.prompt: Which person does Brutus insist should be left out of the conspiracy, saying he would never follow what others begin?
options: Metellus Cimber
Trebonius
Cicero
Caius Ligarius
questions.answer: Cicero.
questions.explanation: In II.i Metellus suggests inviting Cicero for his age and reputation, but Brutus refuses and the others agree.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing Cicero with Cinna, who is one of the conspirators.

questions.prompt: Which argument of Decius helps to change Caesar's mind about going to the Senate?
options: He gives the dream a favourable meaning and says the Senate may mock Caesar or withdraw the offer of a crown if he stays away
He reminds Caesar that the law requires him to attend
He threatens to report Caesar's absence to Pompey's supporters
He says Antony will go in his place
questions.answer: He gives the dream a favourable meaning and says the Senate may mock Caesar or withdraw the offer of a crown if he stays away.
questions.explanation: Decius flatters Caesar by turning Calpurnia's dream of blood into a sign of Rome drawing life from him, and appeals to his pride.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking Caesar is persuaded by a threat. It is flattery and the fear of ridicule that work.

questions.prompt: (a) Who says these words, and to whom? (b) When and where in the play are they spoken? (c) How does the listener respond? (d) Why is this warning important for the rest of the play?
questions.answer: (a) The soothsayer speaks the words to Caesar. (b) They come in I.ii, as Caesar passes through the crowd at the start of the festival procession, in the middle of the games. (c) Caesar has the man brought closer, hears the warning again, calls him a dreamer and moves on. (d) The warning is the first clear sign of danger to Caesar, and it sets a date: the fifteenth of March. Caesar's dismissal is an example of dramatic irony and of his overconfidence, and the soothsayer returns in Act II to try again.
questions.explanation: Cover speaker, listener, situation, reaction and significance. Mention dramatic irony and foreshadowing.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the warning is given by Artemidorus or by Calpurnia.

questions.extract: Yond Cassius has a lean and hungry look; / He thinks too much: such men are dangerous.
questions.prompt: (a) Who speaks these lines, to whom, and about whom? (b) Explain what the speaker means. (c) What does the speaker go on to say about how he feels? (d) What do these lines tell us about the speaker and about Cassius?
questions.answer: (a) Caesar speaks to Antony, about Cassius, in I.ii, after seeing Brutus and Cassius talking together. (b) Caesar means that Cassius looks thin and restless, like a man who is starved of something, and that he thinks too deeply, so he cannot be trusted. (c) Caesar says he is not afraid of Cassius, because he is Caesar, but he says he would rather have plump, easy-going men around him who sleep well. (d) The lines show that Caesar is a sharp judge of character: Cassius is indeed dangerous. They also show his pride, since he claims to have no fear. For Cassius, they suggest envy, ambition and an active mind.
questions.explanation: Speaker, listener and subject; meaning; Caesar's follow-up; and the effect on the audience. Note the irony that Caesar reads Cassius correctly but does not protect himself.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the lines to Brutus or thinking Caesar says them to Cassius directly.

questions.extract: The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings.
questions.prompt: (a) Who speaks these lines and to whom? (b) What does the speaker mean by 'underlings'? (c) What argument is being made, and what is its purpose? (d) How does this speech fit the character of the speaker?
questions.answer: (a) Cassius speaks to Brutus in I.ii, when they are alone during the festival. (b) Underlings are people of lower rank who must obey; Cassius uses the word for Romans who bow to Caesar. (c) He argues that men are not held down by fate or the stars, but by their own lack of courage, so they can change their situation. His purpose is to stir Brutus, who respects the idea of freedom, into thinking that Caesar's rise is Rome's own fault and can be resisted. (d) The speech shows Cassius as a skilful persuader who flatters Brutus, plays on his pride and uses the language of free will. It also expresses his own resentment of Caesar.
questions.explanation: Link the lines to the theme of fate and free will, and to the theme of persuasion.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking Cassius is saying that fate rules everything. He argues the reverse.

questions.extract: It must be by his death
questions.prompt: (a) Who is the speaker, and where and when is it said? (b) Whose death is meant? (c) What reasons does the speaker go on to give? (d) What does the speech reveal about the speaker's character?
questions.answer: (a) Brutus says this in II.i, alone in his orchard at night, in a soliloquy, before the conspirators arrive. (b) He means the death of Caesar. (c) Brutus says he has no personal quarrel with Caesar; the reason is what Caesar might become. Power may change him, as warmth brings a snake to life, so it is safer to stop him before he is crowned. (d) The speech shows Brutus as honest, troubled and reluctant, a man who must reason himself into action. It also shows his weakness: he condemns Caesar for what he might do rather than for what he has done.
questions.explanation: Name the soliloquy device. Mention the snake and the idea of a danger in the future.
questions.commonMistake: Saying Brutus hates Caesar. The speech says the opposite.

questions.extract: Let's be sacrificers, but not butchers, Caius.
questions.prompt: (a) Who speaks and to whom? (b) What has Cassius just proposed? (c) What is the difference between a sacrificer and a butcher, according to Brutus? (d) What does this show about Brutus's view of the plot?
questions.answer: (a) Brutus speaks to Cassius (Caius Cassius) in II.i, in the conspirators' meeting at his house. (b) Cassius has suggested that Antony should be killed along with Caesar. (c) A sacrificer performs a solemn act for a higher purpose; a butcher kills without thought. Brutus wants the plot to look like a noble act, not a slaughter. (d) It shows that Brutus sees the plot as a matter of honour and principle. It also shows his lack of political judgement, because sparing Antony is a mistake that could hurt the conspirators.
questions.explanation: Use the contrast between Brutus's idealism and Cassius's realism.
questions.commonMistake: Missing the reference to Antony.

questions.extract: Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once.
questions.prompt: (a) Who speaks these lines, and to whom? (b) What is the occasion? (c) What does the speaker mean? (d) How does the speech reveal the character of the speaker, and what irony can you find in it?
questions.answer: (a) Caesar speaks to his wife Calpurnia in II.ii, at his house, on the morning of the Ides of March. (b) She has begged him not to go to the Senate because of her dream and the omens. (c) Caesar means that a coward suffers death over and over in his imagination through fear, while a brave man faces death only once, when it actually comes. (d) The lines show Caesar's courage and pride. The irony is that the audience knows the danger is real, and that a man so proud of not fearing death is about to be led by flattery into it. He does not see that ignoring warnings can be foolishness instead of courage.
questions.explanation: Give the occasion, meaning, character and dramatic irony.
questions.commonMistake: Saying Caesar is calling Calpurnia a coward.

questions.extract: When beggars die there are no comets seen; / The heavens themselves blaze forth the death of princes.
questions.prompt: (a) Who speaks these lines, and in what situation? (b) What does the speaker mean? (c) How does Caesar react to this argument? (d) What does the speech show about attitudes to omens in the play?
questions.answer: (a) Calpurnia speaks to Caesar in II.ii, trying to stop him going out after her dream and the strange events of the night. (b) She means that the heavens do not send signs when poor men die, but they announce the deaths of great rulers, so the omens are aimed at Caesar. (c) Caesar does not accept this at first; he insists that a brave man should not be afraid, and only agrees to stay after she kneels and begs. (d) The speech shows the Elizabethan and Roman belief that nature reflects events in the state, and it contrasts Calpurnia's readiness to believe in signs with Caesar's pride and Cicero's scepticism.
questions.explanation: Link the speech to the omens and storm imagery.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing this with Calpurnia's dream of the statue running with blood.

questions.prompt: What happens at the Lupercal festival according to Casca, and why does the shout offstage worry Brutus?
questions.answer: Casca reports that Antony three times offered a crown to Caesar, and that Caesar refused it each time, though Casca thought it seemed half-hearted, and the crowd cheered every refusal. Caesar then fell down in a fit. The shouts heard earlier alarm Brutus because he fears that the people have chosen Caesar as their king, which would end the Republic.
questions.explanation: Include the three offers, the refusals, the crowd's reaction and Brutus's fear.
questions.commonMistake: Saying Caesar accepted the crown.

questions.prompt: Describe the strange happenings of the night of the storm in Act I, scene iii. How do Casca and Cassius interpret them differently?
questions.answer: There is thunder and lightning, and Casca describes a fire in the sky, a slave whose hand burned without harm, a lion wandering in the Capitol area and an owl calling at midday. Casca is terrified and thinks the world is falling apart. Cassius is unafraid, walks openly in the storm and reads the signs as warnings from the gods about the danger of a man like Caesar, which he uses to draw Casca into the plot.
questions.explanation: Give two or three omens and contrast fear with opportunism.
questions.commonMistake: Saying both men read the omens in the same way.

questions.prompt: Why does Brutus refuse to take an oath, and what does this show about him?
questions.answer: When Cassius suggests that the conspirators swear an oath, Brutus refuses. He says that an honest cause needs no oath, and that Romans who are truly honourable will keep their word without one. To ask for an oath would insult their honour and suggest that they doubted their own cause. The refusal shows Brutus's high moral tone and trusting nature, but also that he may be too idealistic about the men he is dealing with.
questions.explanation: State the reason and what it shows about his character.
questions.commonMistake: Saying Brutus refuses because he is unsure about the plot.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the short scene in which Artemidorus reads his letter (Act II, scene iii)?
questions.answer: Artemidorus reads out a letter which names each of the conspirators and warns Caesar to beware of them, saying that they all share one purpose against him. The scene is a moment of suspense, because the audience sees that the plot could still be stopped if Caesar were to read the letter. It also adds to the pattern of warnings ignored, including the soothsayer's, Calpurnia's dream and the omens.
questions.explanation: Mention suspense and the pattern of warnings.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that Caesar reads the letter in this scene.

questions.prompt: Describe how Cassius persuades Brutus to join the conspiracy in Acts I and II. What techniques does he use, and why does he need Brutus?
questions.answer: Cassius knows that the plot needs a man whom Rome trusts, and Brutus is such a man. In I.ii he begins by saying that Brutus has been cold to him, which lets Brutus explain that he is troubled in himself. Cassius then tells Brutus that the Romans respect him and wish he could see himself as others see him, which is flattery. He tells stories of Caesar's weakness, when he nearly drowned in the Tiber and shivered with fever in Spain, to make Caesar seem ordinary. He compares Caesar to a giant statue over a world of small men, arguing that men are underlings by their own fault and not because of fate. The shouts offstage add to the effect, and Brutus admits that he fears a king. Left alone, Cassius plans forged letters, written in many hands, to convince Brutus that Rome is calling him. In I.iii he confirms the plan with Casca and Cinna, saying that Brutus's name will make the plot look honourable. Cassius needs Brutus because his own reputation is poor and Brutus's honour will make the deed look like a service to Rome and not a piece of envy. The persuasion works because Cassius does not create Brutus's doubts, but uses those which already exist. In II.i Brutus is already reasoning himself towards action.
questions.explanation: Cover flattery, Caesar's weaknesses, the appeal to freedom, the forged letters and Brutus's reputation. End with the point that Brutus was already half-persuaded.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that Brutus is tricked entirely by the letters; he is already troubled.

questions.prompt: Compare the characters of Brutus and Cassius as they are shown in Acts I and II.
questions.answer: Brutus and Cassius are allies, but they are very different. Brutus is idealistic and trusting. He loves Caesar but joins the plot for the good of Rome; he wants the deed to be honourable, so he refuses an oath, rejects Cicero and spares Antony. He debates the plot in his mind before he acts. Cassius is practical, envious and quick. He resents Caesar's greatness, uses flattery and forged letters, reads the omens for his own ends, and wants Antony killed for safety. He judges people well and knows how to work on them. Where Brutus thinks in terms of principle, Cassius thinks in terms of results. The contrast shows the two sides of the conspiracy, a noble excuse and a private grievance, and it also hints at tension between them.
questions.explanation: Use paired points with evidence: oath, Antony, motives, attitude to omens.
questions.commonMistake: Listing qualities without linking each to an action.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare use omens, dreams and the storm to build tension in Acts I and II? Refer to at least three examples.
questions.answer: Shakespeare uses signs to create a sense of doom and to show that Rome is disturbed. The soothsayer's warning to beware the Ides of March gives the audience a date. In I.iii the storm, the burning hand, the lion and the owl at noon terrify Casca and make the night seem unnatural. The disturbed night continues into Act II, when Brutus cannot sleep and Caesar's household is restless, and Calpurnia's dream of a statue running with blood and the sacrificed animal without a heart add to the sense of danger. The signs are read differently by different characters: Casca is afraid, Cassius uses them, Calpurnia believes them, Caesar dismisses them and Decius reinterprets them. This creates dramatic irony, for the audience sees the dangers that Caesar ignores, and it keeps the tension high until the end of Act II.
questions.explanation: Give three or more examples, note how different characters read them, and name the effects: foreshadowing, irony and tension.
questions.commonMistake: Describing omens without saying how they affect the audience.

questions.prompt: Brutus says he has no personal reason to act against Caesar and joins the plot only 'for the general good'. Do you think his reasoning is sound? Give reasons with reference to Acts I and II.
questions.answer: Brutus's reasoning is sincere but flawed. In his soliloquy he admits that Caesar has done nothing yet to deserve death, and argues that power may change him; this is a fear about the future, not evidence of guilt. In I.ii Caesar refuses the crown three times, even if some doubt the sincerity of the refusals, and this does not support the claim that he is grasping for a throne. Brutus is also influenced by Cassius's flattery and by the forged letters, which are false, so his decision is partly built on manipulation. On the other side, Brutus does have a serious principle. Rome had driven out kings, and the tribunes and many nobles saw Caesar's rising power as a real threat to shared government. A fair view is that Brutus acts from honour, but honour without careful judgement can lead to serious mistakes, as his choices to trust the conspirators and to spare Antony show.
questions.explanation: Any reasoned view is accepted if it is supported by scenes. Include both sides.
questions.commonMistake: Simply calling Brutus right or wrong without evidence.
